distinguishing_from: vs botwall: status is 200 and the page carries real article metadata plus a subscribe/sign-in offer; a botwall would be 403/202 with under 60 visible-text chars and no article title.
notes: Atypon platform. HTTP 200 with full navigation chrome; the article body itself is replaced by a login offer. body_text_chars stays high (~32k) because of nav/footer boilerplate, so text length alone is NOT a paywall signal here.

distinguishing_from: vs paywall_saas: the purchase language names a single article and an institution, not a seat or plan upgrade.
notes: Also Atypon. 'Restricted access' plus a per-article purchase widget is the strongest academic-paywall pair observed.

distinguishing_from: vs nature_openaccess_NEGATIVE (same site, same template, HTTP 200): the ONLY reliable difference is the JSON-LD isAccessibleForFree value. Nothing in the visible chrome differs.
notes: Best-case machine-readable paywall declaration: schema.org hasPart/cssSelector marks exactly which DOM subtree is gated. Redirect chain 303-302-302-200 through idp.nature.com is an IdP session bounce, NOT a login wall.

distinguishing_from: NEGATIVE CONTROL. Identical template and identical 303/302/302/200 redirect chain to nature_subscription; only isAccessibleForFree flips.
notes: Include in the test corpus as a must-not-fire case. Proves that redirect chains through an identity provider, cookie-error query params, and Nature chrome are all paywall-neutral.
